sections.title: Names: comic, punning and made names
sections.intro: How many of WOTR's names carry a joke, which kinds, who carries them, and whether the world or only the reader hears it. Your PC and the other creators' characters sit outside every option here.

questions.title: How much of the pool is comic
questions.question: What share of new names should be comic, punning or plainly made-up fantasy names?
questions.context: R50-18 dropped the old outlier budget (a cap on names that fit no naming stratum): outliers are now 'free, no ratio, no reason needed'. The struck R23-5 had warned that past its ratio, names read as 'an author picking names he liked'.

options.label: A seasoning
options.consequence: About one comic name in a crowd scene, usually a nickname among the commons. Nearly every other new name stays strict to its bank (a culture's list of name parts).
options.sample: The sergeant read the roll off a slate at the gate of the Seat, his breath standing white in front of each name. Aldric Hale. Ralf Osterby. Dunstan Fenn. Kettle. A short sealer in a hide-coat stepped out at that one, and the column laughed, low, the way men laughed in that cold. The sergeant did not look up. Greta Coll. Nella Ashby. Fern Tolley. The wind came off the rock and took the rest of the laughter with it.

options.label: Most commons and soldiers
options.consequence: Comic bynames and nicknames become the norm in musters, crews, taverns and markets. Above the commons they thin out, and NM4 sets how high they reach.
options.sample: The sergeant read the roll off a slate at the gate of the Seat, his breath standing white in front of each name. Aldric Two-Bowls. Ralf Wetfoot. Dunstan the Lesser, whose brother had been Dunstan the Least. Kettle. Fern Halfpenny. Hob and Dob Garth, who answered together. Nobody in the column laughed. They had heard the roll every morning since the thaw, and the only name that still made a sound among them was the one he skipped.

options.label: About a third
options.consequence: Roughly one new name in three carries a joke, spread across every rank NM4 opens. The rest follow their banks.
options.sample: The sergeant read the roll off a slate at the gate of the Seat, his breath standing white in front of each name. Captain Edric Pinchgauge, on the grey. Aldric Hale. Ralf Wetfoot. Dunstan Fenn. Kettle. Nella Coll. Hob and Dob Garth, who answered together. The captain heard his own name read out in the cold and touched his hat to it, as his father had, and his grandfather, who had at least been a gauger.

options.label: Pratchett density
options.consequence: Most new names carry a joke, as in Discworld, and a strict bank name becomes the exception. Comedy reads as the world's own habit.
options.sample: The sergeant read the roll off a slate at the gate of the Seat. Captain Edric Pinchgauge, on the grey. Aldric Drinkwater. Ralf Wetfoot. Dunstan Gotobed. Kettle. Fern Halfpenny. Nella Breakseal. Hob and Dob Garth, together. Last came Snorin, a Dawi cooper who had signed on for the pay and was asleep on his feet between the shafts of the supply sledge, and the sergeant read his name twice before the man beside him kicked his ankle.

questions.rec_reason: It answers your 'a lot' where the commons live, which is where Norse bynames and English phrase surnames grew in fact, and leaves the reach up the cast to NM4.

questions.title: Built comic names
questions.question: Which kinds of built comic name should WOTR use?
questions.context: R50-17 lets characters 'sound alike', and when they meet 'it becomes a beat'. The Dvergatal, the dwarf-list in the Norse poem Völuspá that Tolkien mined, chimes Fíli with Kíli. Dickens built surnames one notch past believable (Gradgrind), and real English surnames run as odd (Gotobed, Drinkwater).

options.label: Rhyming and alliterating sets
options.consequence: Kin, crews and sworn pairs share a name-part and change the sound, Borin and Snorin style, inside each culture's own sound rules. A set meeting is a beat (R50-17).
options.sample:
Halrin, Kalrin and Valtrin: Kegshard cooper brothers on the shared Dawi element Rin (cut).
Hob and Dob Garth: Northern twins christened with one name, told apart by its two pet forms.
Lu Anping and Lu Anning: lineage-hall cousins sharing the generation syllable An (peace), as the family poem required.

options.label: Dickensian talking surnames
options.consequence: Surnames that tell a trade or a nature one notch past believable, as Gradgrind did: the Victorian imperial register R53-28 already sets, for Northern and Accord families.
options.sample:
Keva Pinchgauge: a Guild inspector whose readings always came out a hair under the meter.
Penn Shortloaf: a baker from a family fined under the assize so often that the fine became the name.
Calla Quillfast: a registry clerk, never once slow.

options.label: Plausible puns, Pratchett-style
options.consequence: Surnames that pass for real ones, with the pun underneath or turned against the bearer. Built from words the Draw Age owns, so no brand, celebrity or modern-world reference.
options.sample:
Niall Lightfoot: a courier with a ruined knee, still the fastest on the Seat road.
Edric Spendlove: a Guild paymaster who never rounded a sum up.
Ivor Drinkwater: sergeant of the driest column in the north, by his own order.

options.label: Phrase and sentence names
options.consequence: A verb and its object frozen into a surname (Shakespeare, Gotobed), and a sect that names its children as moral sentences, as the Puritans did (Sorry-for-sin).
options.sample:
The Breakseals: three generations of honest gaugers, searched at every gate for the name.
Kit Burnoil: of commons who never held a draw licence and said so.
Abide-the-Measure Coll: a child of a strict Guild sect, called Bide by everyone who shared her bunk.

questions.rec_reason: Sets, talking surnames and plausible puns all grow from real naming custom and hold up in a grim room. Sentence names tell the reader what to think of a person on entrance, and the best phrase surnames arrive anyway under C.

questions.title: Grown comic names
questions.question: Which kinds of comic name that grow out of use should WOTR use?
questions.context: A byname is a second name others give for a trade, a look or a deed. R23-2 makes one 'available to anyone' in the Northern stratum, and the naming amendment's Far-Northern section calls bynames 'freely coined'. R50-33 spells a foreigner's bent version of a name 'as heard in dialogue'.

options.label: Soldiers' nicknames
options.consequence: Deed and body bynames from comrades, literal or ironic, the way Abercrombie's Logen Ninefingers counts his missing finger. Peers coin them, so the joke belongs to the characters.
options.sample:
Haldor Two-Bowls: took a second bowl in the Thin Weeks; the laughter stopped when he walked in.
Kitten: the biggest man on the Seat's wall, named by men who later stopped saying it to his face.
Kalvak Twelvecasks: a Dawi cooper; the twelve were the casks he soured.

options.label: Mangled names
options.consequence: A name or phrase bent by a foreign mouth and written as heard, a real mishearing every time (R20-4). Canon already does it: the Dawi say Porin, and Common mouths make it Borin.
options.sample:
Borin: every Common mouth's version of Porin, the softened stops the Dawi call 'voiced', careless speech.
Solly Transit: the Kharven riders' name for any Accord gate clerk, from his 'Solutum et transitum' (paid and passed).
Kettle: a sealer the survey clerk entered by the pot in his hands.

options.label: Sound comedy
options.consequence: Names funny for their noise: hard k sounds, doubled syllables, a goblin mouth's extra consonants. Built inside each people's own sound rules, and most at home among the goblinoids.
options.sample:
Gorrgorr: a goblin porter; gorr is Old Vaross (the goblin tongue) for a load borne, and he bore two.
Gripsnick and Gripsnack: goblin sapper twins, spelled differently by every clerk who met them.
Ukkukk: 'one-one', a goblin fence who always had exactly one left.

options.label: Protective ugly names
options.consequence: A child given a cheap or ugly name so death passes it over, as Chinese and Korean families did; R23-5 already allows a name given 'as an insult or a shield'. Comic to outsiders, grim at home.
options.sample:
Wet Wood: a sickly Kharven girl's name through her first winter, an insult for the cold to hear and a promise for her mother, since wet wood burns eventually.
Gousheng: 'dog's leftovers', a hall elder's milk-name, which his sister still used at seventy in front of the whole hall.

questions.rec_reason: Each grows inside the world out of someone's mouth or custom, so every joke has an owner, which keeps it out of the narration's mouth.

questions.title: Who may carry one
questions.question: How far up the cast may a comic name reach?
questions.context: R52-31 allows 'a comic minor NPC as a comic voice from the start', and R5-D permits 'the joke that is also a threat'. Your PC and the other creators' characters sit outside every option here; that is settled.

options.label: Walk-ons and commons
options.consequence: Comic names stay with one-scene people, crowds, musters and markets. Anyone who recurs gets a strict name.
options.sample:
Dry Tom: a ferryman met once at the ford.
Hob and Dob Garth: two lines on one muster roll.
Kettle: a sealer at a survey post, never seen again.

options.label: Plus recurring NPCs
options.consequence: Recurring minor NPCs (the innkeeper, the sergeant, the Guild clerk) may keep comic names across scenes. Villains and major NPCs stay strict.
options.sample:
Sergeant Ivor Drinkwater: the same dry sergeant through a whole campaign.
Mother Gristle: sold windmeat at the Seat's lower gate on every visit.
Keva Pinchgauge: at every gauge-housing she inspected.

options.label: Plus villains
options.consequence: B, plus villains and rivals, in the Jonson and Dickens line (Volpone the fox, Uriah Heep): a comic name on a dangerous person. Major NPCs keep strict names.
options.sample:
Magister Aulus Tardipes: 'slow-foot' in correct Latin, who signed every death warrant late and never once in error.
Niall Pennywhistle: a Guild factor who bought a district's draw for a song and sold it back by the cup.

options.label: Any rank Natalie makes
options.consequence: Any character Natalie creates, major NPCs included, may carry a comic name. Your PC and the other creators' characters never do.
options.sample:
Halfpint: a Banner House heir his own men named, carrying a full arc.
Old Fumble: a Measurewright across three books, the best reader of Crystals in the north.

questions.rec_reason: A dangerous man with a comic name is the oldest English stage trick and grimdark's best use of the joke that is also a threat; strict names on major NPCs keep the story's weight where it sits.

questions.title: Whose ear hears the joke
questions.question: Must a comic name be a joke someone inside the world can hear, or may some be the reader's alone?
questions.context: R5-C1: 'The narration never winks.' Common, the shared trade tongue, is what the page writes as English, so an English pun is heard in a Common mouth; one buried in a Dawi or Moto name reaches the reader alone. R50-01 makes real-language names 'real, correct phrases'.

options.label: In-world jokes only
options.consequence: Every comic name is funny in its bearer's own tongue or in a Common mouth, and a character glosses it once (says its meaning aloud). Snorin exists only as a Common nickname.
options.sample: The Dawi set his hands flat on the Guild counter and gave his name in his own tongue, Halrin Tharnsson, hard and clean, as if the clerk were auditing him. The clerk wrote it down and thought it sounded noble. Behind the Dawi his foreman laughed into his beard. "The hold calls him Kurlo," he told the clerk, in Common. "Unbegun. It's what he says to every job he's given. Put him on the night casks."

options.label: English puns with a bridge
options.consequence: An English pun is legal where the world supplies a bridge: a Common mouth, a byname rendered in English, or a Common ear mishearing. Reader-only puns hidden in a foreign name stay out.
options.sample: The Dawi set his hands flat on the Guild counter and gave his name in his own tongue, hard and clean, as if the clerk were auditing him. The clerk had not caught a syllable of it. Behind the Dawi the night foreman was already laughing. "Put him down as Snorin," he said. "Everyone does. Sleeps on the cask-stack between shifts." The Dawi did not know the word. He watched the clerk write it in the Concord hand and nodded, gravely, at his new name.

options.label: English puns anywhere
options.consequence: Any name may carry an English pun, foreign given names included (Snorin as a Dawi's own name, an outlier under R50-18). The reader hears it and the characters may not. R5-C1 narrows to narrated remarks.
options.sample: The Dawi set his hands flat on the Guild counter. "Snorin Kalrinsson," he said, hard and clean, as if the clerk were auditing him. The clerk wrote it in the Concord hand and asked for his hold. Kegshard, said Snorin. Cooper. Twelve years on the night casks. Behind him the queue shuffled and coughed in the cold of the hall. The clerk blotted the line, slid the token across, and called the next man.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the no-wink rule, gives you your Snorin today in any Common mouth, and lets the Dawi's own gravity become part of the joke.

questions.title: Which peoples: West and North
questions.question: Among the Dawi, the northern peoples and the goblinoids, which carry comic names?
questions.context: Most peoples already have a comic slot: Northern bynames 'available to anyone' (R23-2), goblinoid bynames 'describing the force that made the person' (R20-1). Dawi given names come from a fixed thirty-element bank (R20-3), and the Dawi call Common's softened stops (Borin for Porin) careless speech.

options.label: The Dawi
options.consequence: Rhyming sets on a shared bank element, deed bynames rendered in English, and outsiders' mangling. Given names stay bank-built; the joke lives in sets, bynames and other people's mouths.
options.sample:
Valtgrim, Kalgrim and Holmgrim: a mining crew on the shared element Grim (forge), the Grims to every foreman.
Kalvak Twelvecasks: the hold entered the soured casks with a straight face.
Bare-chin: canon's Dawi insult for a beard with no rings, no time served.

options.label: Kharven and Far-Northern
options.consequence: Bynames from the Kharven stock of scarcity insults, protective cheap names, and roll-names (surnames an Accord clerk assigned). No joke on the name of the recently dead (R23-11).
options.sample:
Haldor Two-Bowls: the second bowl in the Thin Weeks.
Short-Stack: a lazy man's byname, coined by the neighbours who kept his fire lit.
Bucket: a roll-name a clerk took off the thing in a sealer's hands, paid in tax for three generations.

options.label: Accord and Northern commons
options.consequence: The richest home: talking and phrase surnames, rhyming pet names (Hob and Dob), soldiers' bynames, and Accord jokes in correct Latin (R50-12).
options.sample:
Keva Pinchgauge: a Guild inspector who read light.
Hob and Dob Garth: two pet forms of one name on one roll.
Magister Aulus Tardipes: 'slow-foot' in correct Latin, inspector of couriers.

options.label: Goblinoid peoples
options.consequence: Sound comedy, and bynames whose cause nobody remembers, so a dreaded name can arrive with no story behind it.
options.sample:
Gorrgorr: 'load-load', a porter who carried double.
Gripsnick and Gripsnack: sapper twins.
Grinmaw the Unexplained: feared through three districts, for reasons nobody alive could give.

questions.rec_reason: Each people already has a native comic slot, so the jokes grow from custom. The Dawi keep their given names grave and take their comedy in sets, bynames and other people's mouths.

questions.title: Which peoples: the Eastern strata
questions.question: Among the Japonic houses, the Mahuo and the Chinese lineage halls, which carry comic names?
questions.context: The Japonic houses keep a 'name-taboo on the living' (R23-2), so retainers already go by calling-names, and a Moto given name 'states what the line expects' (R40-1). Names show 'romanised only' (R50-31), so a pun needing written characters never reaches the page. Canon holds one sound pun already: Daigo Tenryū, the Dango Dragon (dango: a rice dumpling).

options.label: Retainers and household staff
options.consequence: Retainers and servants of the Japonic houses take calling-names from real Japanese trait-words, and sound puns on real words, glossed once by a character.
options.sample:
Nebosuke: a gate sentry; the -suke ending made 'sleepyhead' sound like a boy's name.
Kuishinbō: a cook's boy, 'glutton', worn as a calling-name.
The Dango Dragon: canon's own sound pun, on Daigo Tenryū.

options.label: Bloodline cadets, bynames only
options.consequence: Servants and rival Lines coin comic bynames for new cadets of the archaic houses, behind their backs; given names stay under R40-1. No carded Moto is touched, Sodoku least of all, and no Büri form returns.
options.sample:
Lord Lantern: the Shirogane servants' name for a cadet lord nobody saw by day.
Old Inkstone: a Yuno archivist's name in the kitchen, never above stairs.

options.label: The Mahuo
options.consequence: Korean-register names chime through the generation syllable (one syllable every cousin of a generation shares) and can land on a real Korean word; children may carry ugly milk-names. Real Korean only (R50-01).
options.sample:
Dae-chang: 'great prosperity' from the house bank, and the market's word for grilled beef tripe; his cousins all shared the Dae.
Ju-jeong: 'sovereign, correct', said exactly like the Korean for a drunk's rambling.
Gaettong-i: 'dog dung', a Mahuo heir's milk-name, kept now only by his old nurse.

options.label: The Chinese lineage halls
options.consequence: Self-awarded studio names (a scholar's chosen art-name, which other houses mock), insulting posthumous names, cheap child-names and spoken homophone puns. Nothing that needs a written character to land.
options.sample:
Fantong: 'rice bucket', a useless eater's nickname, once written on a Concord contract as a cook's legal name.
Jiuyun Zhai: 'Studio of Nine Clouds', the name an alchemist awarded himself; other halls said Nine Clouds once he left the room.
Gu Huan: 'Gu the Slow', a physician's posthumous name in the hall book, for arriving late at every death.

questions.rec_reason: Each stratum has a real comic custom to draw on. B keeps the ruling houses' given names grave and makes the servants pay for the joke in whispers, which is the joke that is also a threat.

questions.title: Borin Ironheart's rhyming kin
questions.question: Should Borin Ironheart gain a rhyming set of kin or companions, and who makes them?
questions.context: Borin's card names no kin, patronymic (father's name) or oath-name, and says he 'Tells terrible jokes and laughs at them himself'. His name parses from the Dawi bank as Bor (carry) plus Rin (cut), so rhymes on Rin are legal Dawi; Snorin fits no bank element and works only in Common.

options.label: No kin, rhymes elsewhere
options.consequence: Borin's card stays as written. Rhyming Dawi sets appear among new characters, and any set that meets Borin is a beat (R50-17).
options.sample:
Halrin, Kalrin and Valtrin: unrelated Kegshard coopers, whom Borin greeted as long-lost cousins to annoy them.
Borin: unchanged on his card, still laughing at the cooper joke before the punchline.

options.label: Brothers, Snorin included
options.consequence: Natalie invents Borin's brothers on the shared Rin, one called Snorin by every Common mouth, and adds them to his card's kin line once you approve the names.
options.sample:
Torin: the eldest, a hold-reeve (a hold's steward) who had not laughed at one of Borin's jokes in three centuries.
Kalrin: the youngest, a cooper who slept on the cask-stacks, Snorin to every Accord buyer.
Borin: the middle brother, who started the nickname.

options.label: A rhyming forge crew
options.consequence: The Soul Forge's journeymen become a rhyming crew, the Dvergatal habit of chiming companies, and Borin's family stays unwritten. Snorin is the crew's sleeper.
options.sample:
Ymir Rhok: still Borin's Whetstone, outside the rhyme.
Halrin, Valtrin and Kalrin: the night crew at the Soul Forge.
Snorin: what the Accord buyers called Kalrin, who slept on the charcoal sacks.

options.label: You pick from three
options.consequence: Natalie pitches three sets in chat (kin, forge crew, rival smiths), and nothing reaches the card or the page until you pick one.
options.sample:
Set one: brothers on Rin.
Set two: a forge crew on Rin and Grim.
Set three: a rival hold's rhyming smiths, who mocked his jokes.

questions.rec_reason: You named the pair yourself, the shared Rin makes the rhyme legal Dawi, and a brother known as Snorin in Common gives Borin's terrible jokes a target at home.

questions.title: A comic name, a grim end
questions.question: When someone with a comic name dies badly, how does the page carry the name?
questions.context: R49-38 lets 'characters whose humour is their voice' be openly funny, and among the Kharven 'The name of the recently dead is not spoken' until given on (R23-11). Abercrombie's Forley the Weakest dies under his name, and the name makes the death worse.

options.label: Straight, as any death
options.consequence: The name is used plainly and nobody remarks on it; the death gets the same clinical weight as any other. The joke was spent while he lived.
options.sample: The sledge went through at the ford's edge and Snorin went with it, under the shafts, under the ice. They had him out inside a minute. Water had frozen in his beard, and his lips were the blue of snow after sundown. The bonesetter worked his chest until her arms shook. Snorin lay on the bank with his eyes half open and did not move again. Somebody fetched a hide-coat to cover him, and the sledge-team stood steaming in the cold.

options.label: The name turns to grief
options.consequence: Someone says the comic name at the death and the joke becomes the wound. Among the Kharven the name then goes unspoken until it is given on (R23-11).
options.sample: The sledge went through at the ford's edge and Snorin went with it, under the shafts, under the ice. They had him out inside a minute, beard frozen solid, lips gone blue. The bonesetter worked his chest until her arms shook. "Snorin," the foreman said, and shook him by the collar. "Snorin. Up. You've slept enough." He went on saying it after the bonesetter had stopped, until the name was only a sound in the cold.

options.label: Gallows wit at the death
options.consequence: The dying man or his comrades make the joke on his name at the death itself, gallows wit from people whose work earns it (R5-D). The laugh and the death share the beat.
options.sample: The sledge went through at the ford's edge and Snorin came out from under the shafts with his chest stove in. He opened one eye at the foreman. "Don't," he said. "Don't you say it." The foreman said it anyway: that a man called Snorin might have had the manners to die in his sleep. Snorin laughed, once, and blood came up with the laugh, black on the snow, and he did not draw the next breath.

options.label: The true name returns
options.consequence: At the death someone says the true name the comic one covered, and the reader hears it for the first time. The joke stays with the living; the true name goes on the roll of the dead.
options.sample: The sledge went through at the ford's edge and Snorin went with it, under the shafts, under the ice. They had him out inside a minute, beard frozen solid, lips gone blue. The bonesetter worked his chest until her arms shook, and then stopped. The foreman knelt in the slush and said the name the Guild form had never carried, Kalrin Torensson, every stop kept hard, the way the holds said it. Nobody else on that bank had known it.

questions.rec_reason: It is the Forley move: the name the column laughed at becomes the one nobody can stop saying, and the laugh that came before makes the death cost more.

questions.title: Places, inns, ships and gear
questions.question: Beyond people, what may carry a comic name?
questions.context: R50-22 gives a place 'several names, one per culture that uses it', and R50-13 lists an item's names 'side by side'. Technique names stay under R50-11's 'two words at most' and R8-22's literal gloss (the name's flat English meaning).

options.label: Inns, taverns and shops
options.consequence: Signboards and their regulars' nicknames carry the joke, in every culture's towns.
options.sample:
The Drowned Gauger: a draw-district alehouse with a gauge-housing for a sign.
The Honest Measure, called the Short Pint: a tavern by the proof-house.
The Second Bowl: a Kharven eating-house, named in the teeth of the proverb.

options.label: Streets and places
options.consequence: The commons' names for streets, fords and districts sit beside the official ones, one per culture (R50-22). The Accord's Latin name stays grave.
options.sample:
Pinchpenny Row: a street of moneylenders, Via Fenoris (street of interest) on the Accord map.
Dead Horse Ford: no horse had died there in living memory.
The Wet Wood: the Kharven name for an Accord barracks that never kept its word.

options.label: Ships, sledges and engines
options.consequence: Crews' names for vessels, sledge-teams, draw-engines and gun-carriages, beside whatever the registry wrote.
options.sample:
Mabel's Mercy: a river dredger, sunk twice and raised twice.
The Widow's Pace: a supply sledge-team never once late or early.
Old Sulk: a draw-engine at a pumping house that would not start in the cold.

options.label: Weapons and items
options.consequence: Weapons and gear take soldiers' folk names beside their true names (R50-13): the true name in the maker's tongue stays grave, and the folk name may joke. Technique names keep R50-11 and R8-22.
options.sample:
Mother's Spoon: a Kharven sergeant's war-axe, which had stirred worse than broth.
The Argument: a Hallenfeld captain's shotgun, which ended them.
The Magistrate's Cough: a proofed fowling piece that settled debts.

questions.rec_reason: Names on things are the commons' humour at its most natural and land on nobody's dignity, and R50-13 and R50-22 already make room for a folk name beside the true one.

questions.title: Who notices the joke
questions.question: Who on the page may notice that a name is funny?
questions.context: R5-C1: 'The narration never winks', with 'No line acknowledging that the reader knows better.' In close third person the narration runs through one character's head, so what he notices is his. Humour 'arrives inside dialogue and narration already in progress' (R5-D).

options.label: Characters aloud only
options.consequence: Narration uses the name like any other, and only speech touches the joke: a character says it, mocks it or pointedly leaves it alone.
options.sample: The inspector came down the conduit stair with her slate under her arm and the Guild seal on a cord at her neck. "Pinchgauge," she said. "From the proof-house." She read the gauge-housing, wrote a figure, and showed it to Marten. It was a hair under the meter. When she had gone back up the stair the stoker spoke into the firebox. "Pinchgauge. And her father before her." Marten fed the fire.

options.label: Close POV may notice
options.consequence: The POV's own head may register the joke in his own idiom, as he would think it. The narrator outside him never remarks, so R5-C1 stands.
options.sample: The inspector came down the conduit stair with her slate under her arm and the Guild seal on a cord at her neck. "Pinchgauge," she said. "From the proof-house." Of course she was. Marten watched her read the gauge-housing and write a figure, and when she showed it him it was a hair under the meter, and he thought her grandfather had likely read light as well, and his grandfather before him.

options.label: Narration may remark once
options.consequence: At first use the narration may note the joke once, dryly, in its own voice. R5-C1 narrows to its core: no line knowing better than the POV about the plot.
options.sample: The inspector came down the conduit stair with her slate under her arm and the Guild seal on a cord at her neck. Her name was Pinchgauge, and in four generations no Pinchgauge had read a meter high. She read the gauge-housing, wrote a figure, and showed it to Marten. It was a hair under. The family had kept its record.

questions.rec_reason: A close POV noticing is a character noticing, so the no-wink law holds and the joke still lands where you read it.

questions.title: Walk-ons with comic names
questions.question: May a one-scene person carry a comic name before he has spoken twice?
questions.context: R50-27: a new person is 'a role (the gate-clerk) until they speak twice or matter'. Pratchett and Dickens name walk-ons at once, often with the joke as the whole character.

options.label: Role first, as now
options.consequence: R50-27 stands: the walk-on is the gate guard until he speaks twice or matters, and then he gets a name, comic or strict.
options.sample: The gate guard at the lower arch let the cart stand in the wind while he read the seal. He held it upside down for a while, then the right way up, and handed it back with a grunt. "Through." The ox leaned into the traces. Above them on the wall someone bawled down about his supper, and the guard bawled back, and the cart rolled under the arch into the smoke of the outer town.

options.label: Comic name on sight
options.consequence: A walk-on may carry a comic name in narration from his first line, the Pratchett move, while strict names still wait on R50-27. A walk-on named for a joke does not die in that scene.
options.sample: Dozy Wat, who kept the lower arch, let the cart stand in the wind while he read the seal. He held it upside down for a while, then the right way up, and handed it back with a grunt. "Through." The ox leaned into the traces. Above them on the wall someone bawled down about his supper, and Dozy Wat bawled back, and the cart rolled under the arch into the smoke of the outer town.

options.label: Nickname in a mouth
options.consequence: A walk-on may be named at once only by a nickname in someone else's mouth; the narration keeps the role until R50-27 is met. A walk-on named for a joke does not die in that scene.
options.sample: The gate guard at the lower arch let the cart stand in the wind while he read the seal. He held it upside down for a while, then the right way up, and handed it back with a grunt. "Through." The ox leaned into the traces. "Dozy!" someone bawled from the wall. "Your broth's gone to ice!" The guard bawled back, and the cart rolled under the arch into the smoke of the outer town.

questions.rec_reason: Nicknames arrive where soldiers and gate crews really make them, in each other's mouths, and the narration's discipline under R50-27 survives intact.

questions.title: How comic names get made
questions.question: How should comic names be produced at the table?
questions.context: R50-30 lets Natalie 'name by ear to keep the pace', with names checked against the banks and sound rules at scene end. R50-18 already makes a name outside every bank a legal outlier, and R50-28 makes a coined word canon 'only if Isaac reuses it'.

options.label: A comic bank per culture
options.consequence: Each Standing Inventory (the per-culture texture file) gains a comic-name list of bynames, nicknames, rhyming sets and signboards, built in that culture's sound rules.
options.sample:
Kharven: Two-Bowls, Short-Stack, Wet Wood, Full Mouth.
Dawi: sets on Rin, Grim and Tor; Twelvecasks; Kurlo.
Accord and Northern: Pinchgauge, Spendlove, Tardipes, Hob and Dob.

options.label: By ear, sound-checked
options.consequence: Natalie coins comic names live; the scene-end check passes each as an outlier (R50-18) so long as it keeps its culture's sound rules, and flags any that break them.
options.sample:
Dozy Wat: coined at a gate, passed.
Snorin: coined at a Guild counter, passed as a Common nickname.
Gripsnack: passed, since goblin sound rules allowed it.

options.label: A floor per crowd scene
options.consequence: Every scene with a crowd, muster, market or tavern carries at least one comic name, checked by verify_scene (the MCP's draft checker). Quiet scenes and two-handers owe none.
options.sample:
A muster at the Seat: Kettle and the Garth twins.
A Guild hall queue: Snorin.
A death-house Waiting: none owed, none used.

options.label: A pitch list per session
options.consequence: At session start Natalie offers five comic names for the scene's culture and you keep the ones you like; kept names join the bank, and the rest are dropped.
options.sample:
Kharven Seat, tonight: Two-Bowls, Kettle, Dozy Wat, Mother Gristle, the Second Bowl.
Kept: Kettle, Mother Gristle.
Dropped: the rest, unused.

questions.rec_reason: A bank gives each culture's comedy its own sound and keeps it fast at the table, and the sound check stops the scene-end pass failing a good joke. A quota or a nightly vote would turn comedy into a chore.

questions.title: How far the naming law bends
questions.question: How far should comic names bend the current naming rows?
questions.context: The rows in play are the banks (R20-3 Dawi, R37-1 Mahuo, R40-1 Moto), the sound rules (R23-11, R23-10), the walk-on rule R50-27 and the scene-end check R50-30. ME1 decides where the new law is written; this decides what in the naming law changes.

options.label: Inside current law
options.consequence: No row is amended. Comic names live as outliers (R50-18), bynames and nicknames, and any answer above that needs more simply lapses.
options.sample:
R50-27: unchanged.
R50-30: unchanged; comic outliers pass under R50-18.
The banks: unchanged.

options.label: Narrow amendments
options.consequence: Only the rows your answers above bend are amended, each in one line naming its answer: R50-30 for the sound check, R50-27 only if NM12 opens walk-ons. Banks and sound rules stand.
options.sample:
R50-30: amended to pass comic outliers on sound rules alone.
R50-27: amended only if NM12 is B.
The banks: unchanged.

options.label: Banks gain comic slots
options.consequence: B, plus each culture's naming rows gain a comic-names clause pointing to that culture's comic bank in its Standing Inventory, so load_rules serves the bank with the law.
options.sample:
R20-3 (Dawi): gains rhyme sets on a shared element and a byname list.
R23-2 (Northern): gains talking surnames and pet-name pairs.
R23-11 (Far-Northern): gains scarcity bynames and cheap names.

options.label: Comic names exempt
options.consequence: Comic names are exempt from every bank and sound rule (R20-3, R23-11, R40-1) and are checked only for real grammar (R50-01). The banks govern strict names alone.
options.sample:
Snorin as a Dawi given name: legal.
A comic given name for a new Moto cadet: legal.
Any pun: checked for real grammar only.

questions.rec_reason: It matches a comic bank per culture (NM13) and keeps the comedy inside each people's own sound, so the jokes read as the world's habit and the strict names keep their weight.

settled.point: Your PC Sodoku Moto and the other creators' characters (Haruki, Dova'Kan, Gorgi, Ma'Kovu, Fushigi, Xhem, Sonzai) never carry or receive a comic name, and none of them is renamed.
settled.why_not_asked: A standing table rule in NATALIE.md; Sodoku jokes 'only by accident' (R52-14), and the other creators' names belong to them.

settled.point: No comic name revives a Büri or Mongolian-register form; Moto canon governs every joke near the house.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-09-12: the Büri register is dead and the sweep of old pages is in progress.

settled.point: Existing names stay as they are; comic names are for new characters, places and things, and Borin Ironheart keeps his name whatever NM8 decides.
settled.why_not_asked: A published name is corrected for grammar only, 'where the name keeps its sound; the rest stays' (R50-02).

settled.point: A comic name that fits no stratum is a legal outlier, and Natalie may build a comic minor NPC as a comic voice from the start.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law ruled 2026-09-26: outliers are 'free, no ratio, no reason needed'. NM1 asks how many you want, which the law leaves open.

settled.point: A foreigner's bent version of a name is spelled as heard in dialogue, and sound-alike names meeting on the page is a beat.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law; NM2 and NM3 build on both.

settled.point: A pun in a foreign tongue uses real, correct words with a true gloss, and an Accord Latin joke is real Latin.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law ruled 2026-09-26; a comic name gets no exemption.

settled.point: Names show romanised only, so no joke may depend on written characters.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law; NM7 asks only which spoken puns the Eastern strata use.

settled.point: No Earth day or month names in any name, and banned modern slang stays out of narration.
settled.why_not_asked: Live vocabulary law; NM2 option C already keeps brand and celebrity puns out.

settled.point: Every comic name still gets a pronunciation line on its card or place page.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law; a joke name is still a name.

settled.point: Epithets in narration, sobriquets, Third Names, hall titles, honorifics and LitRPG titles.
settled.why_not_asked: Asked in VO4 (epithets), NE1 and NE2 (sobriquets, titles, honorifics) and LR18 (titles); this section takes comic names and nicknames only.
